children: The online gambling industry was last valued at nearly $100B and is expected to double by the early 2030s, fueled by widespread legalization and an advertising blitz that turned every smartphone into pocket-sized casinos.
To fuel that explosive growth, sites like DraftKings
, FanDuel
, Hard Rock Bet, and BetMGM
spend hundreds of millions of dollars on promotional incentives like “Bet & Get,” free spins, and first bet safety nets with as much as $1,500 back in bonus bets if an initial wager loses.
But are these incentives just clever marketing tools to lure in new gamblers or a more nefarious technique to keep the losing bets feeding the online casino's profits?
The New York Times reported on a DraftKings

campaign that allegedly used data science to determine which customers should receive betting incentives based on their win-loss records, while resisting the use of similar technology to identify and protect gamblers most at risk of addiction.
According to a former data analyst interviewed by The New York Times, DraftKings

took customer betting records and built a machine learning model that identifies patterns that could zero in on individuals who were more likely to respond to promotional incentives by gambling and, ultimately, losing more. Each gambler was assigned a score: the higher the score, the more money a gambler was likely to lose for each promotion offered. According to Citizens Bank, DraftKings
spent $3B in promotions but raked in $8.7B in gross revenue.

“We are looking for traits and features that we can target that indicate a good investment,” data analyst Jayden Butts said in the NYT article. By strict financial logic, “the best investment would be a problem gambler.”
The same model could be modified by assigning a risk score to problem gamblers…those most likely to develop addictive and self-destructive gambling problems. But according to Butts, DraftKing
scuttled any efforts to use the model for altruistic purposes, instead doubling down on the "predatory" model of giving losing gamblers more money to spend.
“If you lose more, we give you more, so you keep playing more,” another former analyst said.

The models put gamblers into two categories: elastic and inelastic, with the former marked for fewer promotional incentives, the latter enticed with more “free” money to bet. This identifier was especially useful for slot machines, considered the most addictive form of online gambling.
According to an internal DraftKings
memo in 2023, slots revenue was more elastic than earnings from other games, meaning that promotions were more effective in slots.
To be fair, DraftKings

offers tools for gamblers, including a “cool-off period” which allows users to restrict access to the app for up to a year or self-exclusion lists indefinitely, although those tools are at the discretion of the user, not the company.

The company also follows New Jersey guidelines, which require automatic triggers for specific indications of reckless betting, but has yet to deploy a proactive tool that would identify and possibly disincentivize or block problem gamblers.

In a statement to The New York Times, DraftKings said it “rejects any implication that its marketing practices are unfair or improperly targets customers.” The company disputed how some former employees characterized its use of promotions, saying they are “directed toward customers who demonstrate sustained, engaged use of our platform, not toward customers based on their losses.”
DraftKings
has not yet responded to Seeking Alpha’s request for comment.

title: Is DraftKings betting big on losing gamblers?
